title: The Man Who Tried to Prove Stocks Were a Bad Investment

beats.text: Imagine you set out to prove stocks are a bad investment, and end up fuelling the Roaring Twenties.
It's nineteen twenty-four. You're Edgar Lawrence Smith, and you plan a pamphlet: bonds beat stocks.
You test half a century of real prices, stacking every test in favour of bonds.
Stocks win. Then they win again. Eleven tests, and bonds take one.
How do ordinary shares beat the safest investment in the land?
You see, a farmer sells his crop, but keeps back a sack of seed.
Next year, that seed grows a bigger field.
Good companies do the same, ploughing part of every profit back into the business.
Keynes calls it the book's most important point: compound interest, working for the shareholder.
Then Wall Street reads it, and hears only: stocks always win, at any price.
The seed was real. The price of the field wasn't.

facts.claim: Edgar Lawrence Smith (1882-1971) published Common Stocks as Long Term Investments in 1924
He set out to write a pamphlet showing bonds were the best long-term investment, but the evidence did not support it (own words, Harvard reunion book; NYT Feb 1925)
Tests spanned roughly half a century of prices (from 1866 to 1922; Keynes: 'the past fifty years')
Tests were designed to favour bonds ('every advantage given to bonds'; 'calculated to favor bonds')
Stocks came out ahead in ten of eleven tests; bonds won only one (Test 6, 1866-1885)

Smith's key point: companies retain part of earnings and reinvest them, a compounding effect for shareholders; Keynes called it 'perhaps Mr. Smith's most important, and certainly his most novel, point' and wrote of 'an element of compound interest operating in favour of a sound industrial investment'
Keynes reviewed the book in 1925 (The Nation and Athenaeum)
The book became an intellectual support for the 1920s boom; Fisher and Graham said it influenced market psychology before the Great Crash of October 1929
Farmer/seed analogy is an illustration, not a fact claim

caption:
1924: Edgar Lawrence Smith tried to prove bonds beat stocks. Over half a century of data, stocks won 10 of his 11 tests.
Keynes said the key was profits companies keep and reinvest. Wall Street heard only: stocks always win. Then came 1929.
